nodes.label: Quadratic Equations and Polynomial Theory
nodes.note: Quadratics are the most reliable scoring area in JEE Main algebra: Vieta, discriminant, location of roots and common roots appear in nearly every shift. The same machinery extends to cubics and rational functions.

nodes.label: Polynomials and Identities
nodes.note: Degree, the fundamental theorem and the equation-versus-identity distinction. Skipping the degree check is the most common way to lose an easy question.

nodes.label: Degree and the Fundamental Theorem
nodes.note: $P(x) = a_{n}x^{n} + \dots + a_{1}x + a_{0}$ with $a_{n} \neq 0$ has exactly $n$ roots in $\mathbb{C}$, so $P(x) = a_{n}(x-\alpha_{1})(x-\alpha_{2})\cdots(x-\alpha_{n})$. Degree counts roots with multiplicity.

nodes.label: Equation vs Polynomial
nodes.note: $P(x) = 0$ is an equation with finitely many solutions, while $P(x) \equiv 0$ is an identity true for every $x$. If $a = 0$ in $ax^{2}+bx+c=0$ the degree drops and the quadratic formula becomes illegal.

nodes.label: Identity Theorem
nodes.note: $P(x) \equiv 0$ holds iff every coefficient is zero, so a quadratic satisfied by three distinct values forces $a = 0$, $b = 0$ and $c = 0$. A degree $n$ identity needs only $n+1$ test values to be proven.

nodes.label: Example: Proving an Identity
nodes.note: $\frac{(x-b)(x-c)}{(a-b)(a-c)} + \frac{(x-c)(x-a)}{(b-c)(b-a)} + \frac{(x-a)(x-b)}{(c-a)(c-b)} = 1$ holds at $x = a$, $x = b$ and $x = c$, so by the identity theorem it holds for all real $x$.

nodes.label: Parameterised Leading Coefficient
nodes.note: For $(\lambda-2)x^{2} + 2\lambda x + (\lambda-1) = 0$ first split into $\lambda = 2$, which is linear with one root, and $\lambda \neq 2$, which is quadratic with $D \ge 0$. Testing the discriminant alone misses the linear case.

nodes.label: Roots and Coefficients
nodes.note: Vieta's relations turn questions about roots into arithmetic on coefficients, with no need to solve the equation.

nodes.label: The Quadratic Formula
nodes.note: Completing the square gives $\left(x+\frac{b}{2a}\right)^{2} = \frac{D}{4a^{2}}$, hence $x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{D}}{2a}$ with $D = b^{2}-4ac$. Everything else in the chapter is built on this line.

nodes.label: Sum and Product of Roots
nodes.note: $\alpha + \beta = -\frac{b}{a}$ and $\alpha\beta = \frac{c}{a}$. Any symmetric condition on the roots can be rewritten using only these two numbers.

nodes.label: Difference of Roots
nodes.note: $|\alpha - \beta| = \frac{\sqrt{D}}{|a|}$, coming from $(\alpha-\beta)^{2} = (\alpha+\beta)^{2} - 4\alpha\beta$. Use it whenever the distance between roots is asked.

nodes.label: Transformation of Equations
nodes.note: Roots $\alpha+k$ come from $x = y-k$, roots $k\alpha$ from $x = y/k$, and reciprocal roots from $x = 1/y$. Substitute backwards into the original equation.

nodes.label: Example: Reciprocal Roots
nodes.note: Replacing $x$ by $1/y$ in $ax^{2}+bx+c=0$ and clearing denominators gives $cy^{2}+by+a=0$, whose roots are $\frac{1}{\alpha}$ and $\frac{1}{\beta}$. The coefficients simply reverse.

nodes.label: Sign Conditions on Roots
nodes.note: Roots of opposite signs require only $\frac{c}{a} < 0$, which already forces $D > 0$. Both roots positive need $D \ge 0$ together with $-\frac{b}{2a} > 0$ and $\frac{c}{a} > 0$.

nodes.label: Symmetric Functions and Newton's Sums
nodes.note: Rewriting power sums of roots in terms of $S = \alpha+\beta$ and $P = \alpha\beta$, and the recurrence that generates them.

nodes.label: Symmetric Functions of Roots
nodes.note: $\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2} = S^{2}-2P$, $\frac{1}{\alpha}+\frac{1}{\beta} = \frac{S}{P}$ and $\frac{\alpha}{\beta}+\frac{\beta}{\alpha} = \frac{S^{2}-2P}{P}$. Symmetry is what allows expression purely in $S$ and $P$.

nodes.label: Higher Power Sums
nodes.note: $\alpha^{3}+\beta^{3} = S^{3}-3SP$ and $\alpha^{4}+\beta^{4} = (S^{2}-2P)^{2} - 2P^{2}$. Expand from $S$ and $P$ rather than computing the roots.

nodes.label: Newton's Sums
nodes.note: For $S_{n} = p\alpha^{n} + q\beta^{n}$ the recurrence $aS_{n} + bS_{n-1} + cS_{n-2} = 0$ holds for every integer $n$. It answers very high powers without ever finding $\alpha$ or $\beta$.

nodes.label: Example: Running the Recurrence
nodes.note: With $S_{n} = \alpha^{n}+\beta^{n}$ the recurrence reads $S_{n} = -\frac{b}{a}S_{n-1} - \frac{c}{a}S_{n-2}$, seeded by $S_{0} = 2$ and $S_{1} = -\frac{b}{a}$. Two seeds generate every later term.

nodes.label: Nature of Roots
nodes.note: What the discriminant and the coefficient field together say about the roots, including the pairing theorems and their traps.

nodes.label: Real Field Classification
nodes.note: $D > 0$ gives real distinct roots, $D = 0$ gives the repeated root $-\frac{b}{2a}$, and $D < 0$ gives the conjugate pair $p \pm iq$ with $p = -\frac{b}{2a}$. Geometrically it is two cuts, one touch, or no touch of the $x$-axis.

nodes.label: Rational and Surd Roots
nodes.note: For $a, b, c \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $D > 0$, a perfect square $D$ gives rational roots and a non-square $D$ gives the surd pair $p \pm \sqrt{q}$. Surds therefore never appear alone.

nodes.label: Integral Root Conditions
nodes.note: Integer roots need $a, b, c \in \mathbb{Z}$ with $a = 1$ or $a$ dividing both $b$ and $c$, plus $D$ a perfect square. All three conditions together, not just the last one.

nodes.label: Conjugate Pair Theorems
nodes.note: Real coefficients force complex roots in pairs $z, \bar z$, and rational coefficients force surd pairs $p+\sqrt{q}, p-\sqrt{q}$. The pairing fails the moment coefficients leave that field.

nodes.label: The Conjugate Root Trap
nodes.note: $x^{2} - (2+i)x + (1+i) = 0$ has roots $1$ and $1+i$, with no conjugate present, because the coefficients are complex. Always check the field before invoking conjugate pairing.

nodes.label: Graph of a Quadratic
nodes.note: The parabola, its vertex, sign chart and range. Nearly every inequality question is answered by reading this picture.

nodes.label: Vertex and Axis
nodes.note: Completing the square gives $y = a\left(x+\frac{b}{2a}\right)^{2} - \frac{D}{4a}$, so the vertex is $V\left(-\frac{b}{2a}, -\frac{D}{4a}\right)$ and the axis is $x = -\frac{b}{2a}$.

nodes.label: Sign Chart with Two Roots
nodes.note: For $a > 0$ and roots $\alpha < \beta$, the expression is negative inside $(\alpha, \beta)$ and positive outside it. Reverse every sign when $a < 0$.

nodes.label: Strict Positivity Invariant
nodes.note: $ax^{2}+bx+c > 0$ for every real $x$ iff $a > 0$ and $D < 0$; it is always negative iff $a < 0$ and $D < 0$. Two conditions, always both required.

nodes.label: Example: Always Positive
nodes.note: For $x^{2}+x+1$ we get $D = 1-4 = -3 < 0$ with $a = 1 > 0$, so the curve floats above the axis and $x^{2}+x+1 > 0$ for all real $x$. It never vanishes.

nodes.label: Range on a Restricted Domain
nodes.note: On $[x_{1}, x_{2}]$ compare the endpoint values with the vertex value $-\frac{D}{4a}$ if $x_{v} = -\frac{b}{2a}$ lies inside the interval. Otherwise the function is monotone there and endpoints suffice.

nodes.label: Intercepts
nodes.note: The $y$-intercept is $(0, c)$ and the $x$-intercepts are $\left(\frac{-b \pm \sqrt{D}}{2a}, 0\right)$. When $D < 0$ the parabola meets neither axis except at $c$.

nodes.label: Location of Roots
nodes.note: The canonical conditions for placing roots relative to a point or an interval. Each regime combines the discriminant, the vertex and one sign test.

nodes.label: Both Roots Beyond a Point k
nodes.note: $\alpha, \beta > k$ needs $D \ge 0$, $-\frac{b}{2a} > k$ and $af(k) > 0$; for $\alpha, \beta < k$ the middle condition flips to $-\frac{b}{2a} < k$. Three conditions intersected.

nodes.label: k Between the Roots
nodes.note: $\alpha < k < \beta$ is captured by the single condition $af(k) < 0$, which automatically forces $D > 0$. This is the shortest condition in the whole topic.

nodes.label: Both Roots Inside an Interval
nodes.note: Roots inside $(k_{1}, k_{2})$ need $D \ge 0$, $k_{1} < -\frac{b}{2a} < k_{2}$, $af(k_{1}) > 0$ and $af(k_{2}) > 0$. Real roots, the vertex and both endpoints are all constrained.

nodes.label: Exactly One Root in an Interval
nodes.note: Exactly one root in the open interval $(k_{1}, k_{2})$ is simply $f(k_{1}) \cdot f(k_{2}) < 0$, since the curve must cross zero between the endpoints. Handle endpoints that are roots separately.

nodes.label: Interval Between the Roots
nodes.note: $\alpha < k_{1} < k_{2} < \beta$ needs $af(k_{1}) < 0$ and $af(k_{2}) < 0$, and either one already implies $D > 0$. The interval then sits in the negative well of an upward parabola.

nodes.label: Common Roots
nodes.note: Two quadratics sharing roots, decided either by an eliminant or by proportionality of coefficients.

nodes.label: Both Roots Common
nodes.note: Both roots are shared iff the coefficient triples are proportional: $\frac{a_{1}}{a_{2}} = \frac{b_{1}}{b_{2}} = \frac{c_{1}}{c_{2}}$. The two equations then describe the same parabola scaled.

nodes.label: Subtraction Gives a Candidate
nodes.note: Subtracting $x^{2}+ax+b=0$ and $x^{2}+cx+d=0$ yields the candidate $x = \frac{d-b}{a-c}$, which must be substituted back. If $a = c$ and $b \neq d$ there is no common root at all.

nodes.label: Complex Common Root Trap
nodes.note: If the first equation has real coefficients and $D_{1} < 0$, a shared complex root forces the conjugate to be shared too, so both roots are common and $\frac{a_{1}}{a_{2}} = \frac{b_{1}}{b_{2}} = \frac{c_{1}}{c_{2}}$.

nodes.label: Range of Rational Functions
nodes.note: Finding the range of a ratio of quadratics by reversing the problem into a discriminant condition on the numerator.

nodes.label: Discriminant Inversion
nodes.note: Cross-multiplying $y = \frac{a_{1}x^{2}+b_{1}x+c_{1}}{a_{2}x^{2}+b_{2}x+c_{2}}$ gives $(ya_{2}-a_{1})x^{2} + (yb_{2}-b_{1})x + (yc_{2}-c_{1}) = 0$, and requiring $D_{x} \ge 0$ yields an inequality in $y$ for the range.

nodes.label: Boundary and Asymptote Check
nodes.note: The candidate $y = \frac{a_{1}}{a_{2}}$, where the coefficient of $x^{2}$ dies, must be tested separately by substituting back into the linear equation. It is the horizontal asymptote $\lim_{x \to \pm\infty} y$.

nodes.label: Removable Common Factor Trap
nodes.note: If $(x-k)$ cancels from numerator and denominator, the graph has a hole at $x = k$ and the value $\frac{k-\alpha}{k-\beta}$ is never attained. Delete it from the otherwise computed range.

nodes.label: Higher Degree Polynomials
nodes.note: Generalised Vieta, cubics, roots in progressions and sign counting. The same symmetric-function logic simply scales up.

nodes.label: Generalised Vieta Formulas
nodes.note: For degree $n$, $\sum \alpha_{i} = -\frac{a_{n-1}}{a_{n}}$, $\sum_{i<j}\alpha_{i}\alpha_{j} = \frac{a_{n-2}}{a_{n}}$ and $\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}\cdots\alpha_{n} = (-1)^{n}\frac{a_{0}}{a_{n}}$. Signs alternate from the top.

nodes.label: Cubic Equations
nodes.note: For $ax^{3}+bx^{2}+cx+d=0$ the roots obey $\alpha+\beta+\gamma = -\frac{b}{a}$, $\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha = \frac{c}{a}$ and $\alpha\beta\gamma = -\frac{d}{a}$.

nodes.label: Roots in AP, GP and HP
nodes.note: For roots in AP assume $t-d, t, t+d$, giving $t = -\frac{b}{3a}$; for GP use $\frac{t}{r}, t, tr$, giving $t^{3} = -\frac{d}{a}$; for HP substitute $x = \frac{1}{y}$ to get roots in AP.

nodes.label: Descartes' Rule of Signs
nodes.note: The number of positive real roots equals the sign changes among non-zero coefficients of $P(x)$, or is less by an even number; for negative roots apply the rule to $P(-x)$.

nodes.label: Turning Points
nodes.note: $P'(x) = 0$ locates the local extrema, so a degree $n$ polynomial has at most $n-1$ turning points. Between two distinct real roots there is always one turning point.

nodes.label: Reducible and Symmetric Equations
nodes.note: Higher-degree equations that collapse into a quadratic after a smart substitution.

nodes.label: Reciprocal (Palindromic) Equations
nodes.note: For $ax^{4}+bx^{3}+cx^{2}+bx+a=0$ divide by $x^{2}$ and set $u = x + \frac{1}{x}$, using $x^{2} + \frac{1}{x^{2}} = u^{2}-2$. The quartic becomes a quadratic in $u$.

nodes.label: The |u| >= 2 Condition
nodes.note: Solving $x + \frac{1}{x} = u$ gives real $x$ iff $|u| \ge 2$, and for $|u| < 2$ the roots are non-real conjugates. Reject the $u$ values that fail this test.

nodes.label: Equations with a Modulus
nodes.note: In $ax^{2}+b|x|+c=0$ substitute $u = |x| \ge 0$ and solve for $u$. Each $u > 0$ yields two roots $x = \pm u$, $u = 0$ yields one, and negative $u$ yields none.

nodes.label: Example: Counting Roots
nodes.note: For $x^{2} - 5|x| + 6 = 0$ the substitution gives $u = 2$ or $u = 3$, so there are four real roots $\pm 2$ and $\pm 3$. Count in $u$ first, then translate back to $x$.
